cues.text: Around the year 1400, Father Arnoldus Groen was celebrating Mass in the church of Sts. Peter and Paul at Boxmeer, in the Netherlands.
Immediately after pronouncing the words of consecration, he was overtaken by a sudden and unwelcome doubt about the Real Presence of Christ in the bread and wine he had just consecrated.
Without warning, the consecrated wine began to bubble up out of the chalice on its own, splashing onto the corporal — the small linen cloth spread beneath the sacred vessels.
Terrified at what he was witnessing, Father Groen immediately asked God's forgiveness for his doubt, and as soon as he did, the bubbling stopped.

The wine that had spilled onto the corporal coagulated into a solid lump of blood roughly the size of a walnut, and rather than being discarded or hidden, the stained corporal was preserved as a relic of the event.
It was later fitted into a cylindrical reliquary in 1482, and a protective container was built for that reliquary in 1650.
This suggests continuous, deliberate veneration across nearly three centuries before either object survives into the modern historical record with any real documentary detail.
The relic drew the personal devotion of later popes, including Clement XI, Benedict XIV, Pius IX, and Leo XIII.
In 2000, Pope John Paul II elevated the church at Boxmeer to basilica rank, partly recognizing the shrine it had become.
The stained corporal remains on display for veneration in what is now the crypt of the Basilica of St. Peter at Boxmeer.

The Boxmeer account belongs to a familiar pattern among Eucharistic miracle traditions — a priest's private, unspoken doubt met not with condemnation but with a visible sign, followed by his own immediate repentance rather than any punishment.
The devotion has remained alive for over six centuries because of the plain physical relic it left behind.
It is still shown today exactly where the corporal first caught the wine that would not stay ordinary.
